title: Cognitive distortions (thinking traps)
description: Systematic errors in how automatic thoughts process information (how a thought is biased, not what it is about). Tags automatic thoughts and hot thoughts in five-part, cognitive model and thought record formulation slots. Overlaps resolved: tunnel vision is an alias of mental filter, probability overestimation of fortune telling, awfulizing of catastrophizing.

concepts.label: All-or-nothing thinking
concepts.definition: Viewing a situation, person or self in only two extreme categories instead of on a continuum, so anything short of perfect counts as failure.
concepts.client_wording: Seeing things as all good or all bad, with nothing in between.
concepts.example: "If I don't get an A, I'm a total failure."
sources: Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts (thinking errors)
Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)
Beck-1963 § Cognitive distortions

concepts.label: Overgeneralization
concepts.definition: Drawing a sweeping negative conclusion from a single event or a few events, often signaled by words such as always, never or everyone.
concepts.client_wording: Treating one bad experience as proof that it will always happen.
concepts.example: "I got turned down again. Nobody will ever want to go out with me."
sources: Beck-1963 § Cognitive distortions
Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)
Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts (thinking errors)

concepts.label: Labeling
concepts.definition: Attaching a fixed, global, usually harsh label to oneself or others on the basis of particular behaviors, instead of describing the behavior.
concepts.client_wording: Calling yourself or someone else a name, like loser or idiot, because of one thing.
concepts.example: "I forgot her birthday. I'm a terrible friend."
sources: Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)
Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts (thinking errors)

concepts.label: Mental filter
concepts.definition: Attending to one negative detail, or only to the negative aspects of a situation, and judging the whole by them while overlooking the rest.
concepts.client_wording: Focusing on the one thing that went wrong and missing everything that went right.
concepts.example: Ten people praise a talk and one criticizes it; the client thinks only "It went badly."
sources: Beck-1963 § Cognitive distortions
Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)
Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts (thinking errors)

concepts.label: Disqualifying the positive
concepts.definition: Rejecting positive experiences, qualities or feedback as not counting, for example by crediting luck or kindness, so negative beliefs stay intact.
concepts.client_wording: Brushing off good things or compliments as flukes that don't really count.
concepts.example: "She only said it went well because she was being nice."
sources: Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)
Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts (thinking errors)

concepts.label: Magnification and minimization
concepts.definition: Exaggerating the importance of negatives, such as one's mistakes or others' strengths, while shrinking the importance of positives, such as one's own strengths.
concepts.client_wording: Blowing your mistakes out of proportion while shrinking your strengths and successes.
concepts.example: "One typo ruined the whole report. Finishing it early means nothing."
sources: Beck-1963 § Cognitive distortions
Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)
Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts (thinking errors)

concepts.label: Jumping to conclusions
concepts.definition: Reaching a negative conclusion without adequate evidence, or despite contrary evidence. Umbrella term for mind reading and fortune telling.
concepts.client_wording: Deciding something bad is true before you have the facts.
concepts.example: "He hasn't replied to my text. I must have upset him."
sources: Beck-1963 § Cognitive distortions
Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)
Beck-etal-2024 § Ch. 1 Overview

concepts.label: Mind reading
concepts.definition: Assuming you know what others are thinking, usually that they judge you negatively, without checking or considering other possibilities.
concepts.client_wording: Being sure you know what others think of you, without asking.
concepts.example: "Everyone in the meeting thinks I'm boring."
sources: Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)
Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts (thinking errors)

concepts.label: Fortune telling
concepts.definition: Predicting a negative outcome as if it were certain, or judging a feared outcome far more likely than the evidence suggests.
concepts.client_wording: Predicting things will go badly and treating the prediction as a fact.
concepts.example: "I'll freeze in the interview and won't get the job."
sources: Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)
Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts (thinking errors)
Clark-2009 § Introduction (overestimates of danger)

concepts.label: Emotional reasoning
concepts.definition: Taking one's feelings as evidence of how things really are, reasoning that because something feels true, it must be true.
concepts.client_wording: Believing something is true just because it feels true.
concepts.example: "I feel so anxious, something terrible must be about to happen."
sources: Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)
Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts (thinking errors)
Clark-Beck-2010 § Ch. 2 The Cognitive Model of Anxiety

concepts.label: Catastrophizing
concepts.definition: Imagining or expecting the worst possible outcome and judging it unbearable, overestimating how severe the consequences of an event would be.
concepts.client_wording: Jumping to the worst-case scenario and believing it would be a disaster you couldn't survive.
concepts.example: "If I lose this job, I'll lose the house and end up on the street."
sources: Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts (thinking errors)
Clark-Beck-2010 § Ch. 2 The Cognitive Model of Anxiety
Clark-2009 § Introduction (overestimates of danger)

concepts.label: Underestimating coping
concepts.definition: Underrating one's ability to cope with a feared event and overlooking available help or rescue factors, which magnifies perceived threat.
concepts.client_wording: Believing you couldn't handle it if something bad happened, and that no one would help.
concepts.example: "If I get anxious at the party, I won't be able to handle it."
sources: Clark-2009 § Introduction (overestimates of danger)
Clark-Beck-2010 § Ch. 2 The Cognitive Model of Anxiety

concepts.label: Should statements
concepts.definition: Holding rigid, absolute demands about how oneself, others or the world should or must be. Unmet demands bring guilt, frustration or anger.
concepts.client_wording: Having strict rules about how you or others must act, and feeling bad when they're broken.
concepts.example: "I should never make mistakes." "He ought to know how I feel."
sources: Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)
Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts (thinking errors)

concepts.label: Low frustration tolerance
concepts.definition: Believing that frustration, discomfort or unpleasant emotion is unbearable and must be avoided or ended at once, rather than unpleasant but tolerable.
concepts.client_wording: Telling yourself you can't stand feeling uncomfortable or frustrated, even for a short while.
concepts.example: "I can't stand waiting. This is unbearable."
sources: Harrington-2005 § Frustration intolerance beliefs (Frustration Discomfort Scale)

concepts.label: Personalization
concepts.definition: Believing you caused, or are the target of, negative events or others' behavior without considering other, more likely explanations.
concepts.client_wording: Assuming bad things are your fault or about you, when other reasons are more likely.
concepts.example: "My son failed his test because I'm a bad mother."
sources: Beck-1963 § Cognitive distortions
Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)
Beck-2021 § Ch. 14 Evaluating Automatic Thoughts (thinking errors)

concepts.label: Blaming
concepts.definition: Holding other people or circumstances entirely responsible for one's problems or feelings, overlooking one's own part and what one can change.
concepts.client_wording: Putting all the blame for a problem on someone else, and missing what you can change.
concepts.example: "My partner is the reason I'm miserable."
sources: Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think (cognitive distortions)

concepts.label: Hindsight bias
concepts.definition: Judging past decisions with knowledge gained only afterward, believing the outcome was foreseeable and preventable at the time. Common in trauma-related guilt.
concepts.client_wording: Blaming yourself for not knowing back then what you only found out later.
concepts.example: "I should have known he was dangerous and left sooner."
sources: Kubany-Manke-1995 § Hindsight bias
Resick-etal-2024 § Assimilation and hindsight bias (stuck points)
PsychologyTools-CognitiveDistortions § Hindsight bias

concepts.label: Unfair comparisons
concepts.definition: Comparing oneself selectively with people who seem better off, or with unrealistic standards, and concluding one is inferior or lacking.
concepts.client_wording: Measuring yourself against people who seem to be doing better and feeling you come up short.
concepts.example: "Everyone my age has a house and kids. I've achieved nothing."
sources: Gilbert-1998 § Social comparison
PsychologyTools-CognitiveDistortions § Social comparison

concepts.label: Overly optimistic thinking
concepts.definition: Unrealistically positive predictions about time, effort, ability or future motivation that feel good now but lead to delay and less skill use.
concepts.client_wording: Telling yourself a task will be quick or easy later, so you don't start now.
concepts.example: "It'll only take twenty minutes. I can easily start tonight."
sources: Knouse-Mitchell-2015 § Positively-valenced cognitive avoidance: a functional analysis
Knouse-etal-2019 § Introduction

concepts.label: Permission-giving thoughts
concepts.definition: Thoughts that justify putting off a task or giving in to an urge, bringing short-term relief and so reinforcing avoidance.
concepts.client_wording: Thoughts that give you a reason to put something off, like 'I'll just do this first.'
concepts.example: "I'll feel more like doing it after I check my email."
sources: Knouse-etal-2019 § Introduction (permission-giving thoughts)
Knouse-Mitchell-2015 § Avoidance function of overly positive thoughts
Beck-etal-1993 § Permission-giving beliefs
